summary.text: Molecular biology is the branch of biology that studies the molecular structures and chemical processes behind biological activity inside and between cells.
It centers largely on nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA and on proteins, and on how these macromolecules carry out replication, transcription and translation.
Its techniques are used to target new drugs, diagnose disease, and better understand how cells work.

items.prompt: A lab measures the purines in a DNA sample (adenine plus guanine). What should the pyrimidines (cytosine plus thymine) total?

options.label: About half as much as the purines
Double the purines
The same amount as the purines
Nothing, since they occur only in RNA

items.explain: Chargaff found that the total concentration of purines is always equal to that of pyrimidines.

items.prompt: A stretch of a gene's DNA is 12 bases long, read from a fixed start with no overlap, and codes for part of a protein. How many amino acids does it specify?

options.label: Four amino acids
Twelve amino acids
Six amino acids
Three amino acids

items.explain: Each triplet of bases (a codon) specifies one amino acid, and codons do not overlap, so 12 bases give 4.

items.prompt: Researchers tag a virus's protein coat with one radioactive marker and its genetic material with another, then let it infect bacteria. What did this show?

options.label: The protein coat carried all the instructions for making new viruses
The bacteria supplied the instructions and the virus supplied none
Coat and genetic material were equally needed to make new viruses
The genetic material injected held everything needed to make new viruses

items.explain: Hershey and Chase showed the DNA injected by a phage contains all the information needed to make progeny phage.

items.prompt: Cells were seen under microscopes in the 1700s, yet how they work at the molecular level stayed unclear for two centuries. What finally changed?

options.label: Biologists dropped whole organisms and began studying only single cells
Tools from physics and chemistry advanced enough to be used on biology problems
A new law of inheritance was found in pea plants
Cells were seen for the very first time under a microscope

items.explain: Detailed understanding of cell mechanisms arrived in the 20th century once physics and chemistry technologies could be applied to biology.

items.prompt: A biochemist studies pus-filled bandages and isolates a phosphorus-containing substance he calls nuclein. What do we now know it to be?

options.label: A protein from bacteria
A sugar capsule
A fat-like wax
DNA

items.explain: Friedrich Miescher's nuclein is now known to be DNA.

items.prompt: Why does a host's immune system fail against smooth-strain pneumococcus but beat the rough strain?

options.label: The rough strain's capsule makes it far easier for the host to attack
The smooth strain lacks any coat, so the immune system overlooks it
The smooth strain's polysaccharide capsule keeps the immune system from recognizing it
The rough strain makes antigens that smooth strains cannot produce

items.explain: The polysaccharide capsule hides smooth bacteria from the immune system, while the capsule-free rough strain is readily recognized and destroyed.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about the genetic code is wrong. Which?

steps.text: A gene's DNA specifies the amino acids of a protein.
Each successive amino acid is specified by three sequential bases.
So the code is a triplet code, and each triplet is called a codon.
Codons overlap, so each base helps specify several amino acids.

beats.explain: The codons were shown not to overlap, and each sequence is read from a fixed starting point.

beats.idea: Experiment by experiment, DNA was shown to carry genetic information in a double helix read three bases at a time.

paragraphs.heading: Life at the scale of molecules
paragraphs.text: Molecular biology tries to explain living things by looking at the molecules inside and between cells and the chemistry they carry out. Most of its attention goes to nucleic acids, such as DNA and RNA, and to proteins. It asks how these big molecules are built, what they do and how they act on one another as a cell copies its DNA, reads its genes and makes proteins. The field borrows from genetics, biochemistry, physics, mathematics and, more lately, computer science, in a branch called bioinformatics.

paragraphs.heading: Why it arrived late
paragraphs.text: Cells and other tiny structures had been spotted in living things as early as the 18th century. Yet a detailed picture of how cells work only came in the 20th century, once tools from physics and chemistry were good enough to turn on living things. Molecular biology grew up where biochemistry and genetics meet, as both fields came to seek the molecular workings behind a cell's vital tasks. Its progress has gone hand in hand with new technologies and their refinement.

paragraphs.heading: The double helix and the code
paragraphs.text: In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick published DNA's double helix, drawing on X-ray crystallography by Rosalind Franklin that reached them through Maurice Wilkins and Max Perutz. They also guessed at what the shape might mean for how DNA is copied. Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. In 1961 it was shown that a gene spells out a protein three DNA letters at a time, each triplet, or codon, standing for one amino acid, read from a fixed start without overlaps.

paragraphs.heading: Proving genes are DNA
paragraphs.text: In 1928 Frederick Griffith worked with pneumococcus bacteria that were killing lab rats. One strain was smooth and deadly, coated in a polysaccharide capsule that hid it from the host's immune system; the other was rough, lacked the capsule and was easily destroyed. Griffith proposed that genes could pass between members of the same generation, now called genetic transformation. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase confirmed that DNA is the genetic material: working with E. coli and a bacteriophage, they tagged the phage's protein coat and its DNA with different radioactive labels, and found that the DNA a phage injects into a bacterium holds everything needed to build new phages.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters today
paragraphs.text: Molecular biology gives scientists techniques for studying the processes inside cells. Those methods help aim new drugs, diagnose disease and understand how cells function. Some treatments that grew out of the field fall under gene therapy, and its use in medicine is now known as molecular medicine.
